links.note: In July 1054 Cardinal Humbert and two other envoys of the pope cast the patriarch of Constantinople, Michael Cerularius, out of the church. Their written sentence calls him a patriarch in name only. It says the seeds of heresy are sown among his followers every day. Crusaders took Constantinople in 1204. Pope Innocent III then treated its church as his own. In 1205 he wrote that it had lately come back into unity with Rome.

links.note: Around 1100 the emperor Alexios I and the patriarch Nicholas put the Bogomil teacher Basil on trial. Basil would not give up his faith, so the emperor had him burned in the Hippodrome. links.note: In 1215 a great church council at Rome condemned a small book Joachim had written against Peter Lombard's teaching on the Trinity. In 1254 a friar's book built on Joachim's works caused alarm in Paris. A papal panel met at Anagni in 1255 to judge it, and the book was condemned.

links.note: In his Institutes, John Calvin of Geneva wrote against Pope Gregory VII by name. He said Gregory, once called Hildebrand, was the one who first won the popes the rank of emperors. He called him 'an impure and wicked man'. The popes after him, Calvin wrote, went on to rule the emperors.

sources.work: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion IV.11, chapter summary (trans. Beveridge, 1845)

sources.work: John Calvin, Institutes IV.11.13 (trans. Beveridge, 1845)
sources.quote: At length Hildebrand, who took the name of Gre- gory VII., an impure and wicked man, betrayed his sinister intentions.

sources.work: John Calvin, Institutes IV.11.13 (trans. Beveridge, 1845)
sources.quote: He gained this much, hoAvever, that his successors were not only able to shake off the yoke with impunity, but also to bring the emperors into subjection to them.

links.note: Bernard of Clairvaux, the Cistercians' best-known abbot, wrote In Praise of the New Knighthood in defense of the Templars. He argued that a knight who killed in this cause was killing evil, not a man. This rests on the modern history of the order, not on Bernard's own text.

sources.work: Malcolm Barber, The New Knighthood: A History of the Order of the Temple (Cambridge University Press, 1994)

links.note: In March 1312 Pope Clement V issued the bull Vox in excelso, with the approval of a church council. It abolished the order of the Temple for ever. No one was to join it, wear its habit or pass himself off as a Templar, on pain of excommunication.

sources.work: Clement V, bull Vox in excelso (22 March 1312), in Mirbt, Quellen, 3rd ed. (1911), no. 310
sources.quote: districtius inhibentes, ne quis dictum ordinem de caetero intrare, vel eius habitum suscipere vel portare aut pro templario gerere se praesumat.

links.to_name: The Byzantine Church after the Schism
links.note: Vartan, an Armenian historian of the 1200s, says Emperor Manuel asked the catholicos Gregory and his brother Nerses to set out their faith. They wrote it down and sought union with the Greeks, but the work was never finished. Michael the Syrian quotes a letter from Nerses. It lists what the Greeks asked of him, among them belief in two natures in Christ and honor for the fourth council.

links.note: Kirakos of Gandzak wrote a history of Armenia in the 1200s. He tells how Catholicos Gregory III went on pilgrimage. At Antioch the people led him to the throne of Saint Peter. In Jerusalem, Kirakos says, the Franks and their patriarch made their bond with the Armenians stronger than ever.

links.note: Michael the Syrian, a Syriac patriarch who lived through these events, tells how the prince of Antioch brought back a Greek patriarch, Athanasius, from Constantinople. The Latin patriarch, Aimery, left the city and cut its people off from the church. After an earthquake in 1170, Aimery told them to throw the Greek patriarch out 'with contempt' as an intruder.

links.note: William of Tyre was archbishop of Tyre in the crusader kingdom. He wrote that the Maronites joined the Latin church around 1182. This rests on modern historians of the Maronites, not on his own text.

sources.work: Matti Moosa, The Maronites in History (Syracuse University Press, 1986; repr. Gorgias 2005)
Kamal Salibi, Maronite Historians of Mediaeval Lebanon (Beirut, 1959)

links.note: In 1215 the Maronite patriarch Jeremiah al-Amshitti went to Rome for the Fourth Lateran Council. A papal bull then set out the terms of the union. This rests on modern historians of the Maronites, not on the bull or the council's acts.

sources.work: Matti Moosa, The Maronites in History (Syracuse University Press, 1986; repr. Gorgias 2005)

links.to_name: The Latin Papal Church (Gregorian Reform to Innocent III)
links.note: At the Second Council of Lyon in 1274, the Greek side made a profession of faith. In it they accepted the full primacy of the Roman church. Its 1911 editor says Pope Clement IV first put the text to Emperor Michael VIII in 1267. Michael then offered it to Pope Gregory X at Lyon. The profession does not show how the Greek church received the union.

sources.work: Profession of faith of Michael VIII Palaiologos (1274), in Denzinger, Enchiridion symbolorum, ed. Bannwart (1911), on the Roman primacy
sources.quote: quem se ab ipso Domino in beato PETRO Apostolorum principe sive vertice, cuius Romanus Pontifex est successor, cum potestatis plenitudine recepisse veraciter et humiliter recognoscit.

sources.work: First Vatican Council, Pastor aeternus, ch. 4 (1870), on the Greeks' profession at Lyon, in Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, vol. 2 (1878), English
sources.quote: with the approval of the Second Council of Lyons, the Greeks professed that the holy Roman Church enjoys su- preme and full primacy and pre- eminence over the whole Catholic Church,

sources.work: Clemens Bannwart (ed.), Denzinger, Enchiridion symbolorum, 11th ed. (1911), heading and note to nos. 461-466 (the profession of Michael VIII)

links.from_name: The Byzantine Church after the Schism
links.note: The church of Rus' was a province of the church of Constantinople. Mouravieff, a Russian church historian writing in 1838, says its chief bishops were named at Constantinople and answered to the patriarch there. One of them, Matthew, was sent from the city just before the crusaders took it.

sources.work: A. N. Mouravieff, A History of the Church of Russia (1838; trans. R. W. Blackmore, Oxford, 1842)
A. N. Mouravieff, A History of the Church of Russia (1838; trans. R. W. Blackmore, Oxford, 1842)

links.from_name: The Church of the East under the Mongols
links.to_name: The Latin Papal Church (Gregorian Reform to Innocent III)
links.note: Rabban Sawma, a monk of the Church of the East, reached Rome as envoy of the Mongol king Arghun and of his own catholicos. He told the cardinals he carried letters 'concerning the matter of Jerusalem'. He then gave communion to the king of England, probably in Gascony. Back in Rome, he received it from the new pope, Nicholas IV.

sources.work: History of Mar Yahballaha and Rabban Sawma (trans. Budge, The Monks of Kublai Khan, 1928), Sawma before the cardinals in Rome
sources.quote: The Mongols and the Catholicus of the East have sent me to Mar Papa concerning the matter of Jerusalem; and they have sent letters with me.

links.note: Around 1200 a Coptic survey of Egypt's churches says the head bishop of Abyssinia is sent 'from the patriarch of Alexandria'. 'Abd al-Latif, writing in the same years, tells of an envoy from the Abyssinian king. The envoy reported the bishop's death and asked for a new one. A note in the Kebra Nagast names a Coptic book of 'the throne of Mark' in King Lalibela's time.

sources.work: Churches and Monasteries of Egypt, attributed to Abu Salih (trans. Evetts, 1895), on Abyssinia
sources.quote: A metropolitan is sent from the see of Mark the Evangelist to Abyssinia ^, from the patriarch of Alexandria in Egypt ;

links.note: In 1440 Pope Eugenius IV wrote of a hermitage in Spain where Franciscan friars lived. He said they lived under the observance of the Rule of blessed Francis. In 1438 he had confirmed Bernardino of Siena as head of the order's Observant houses in Italy. That letter says the houses were set up 'under the holy name of observance'.
